goals: Explain why ANOVA beats multiple t-tests
why: Comparing three suppliers, four ad creatives or five machine settings is common. Running many t-tests inflates false positives; ANOVA handles all groups in one test.
explain: With 5 groups there are 10 pairwise t-tests. At α = 0.05 each, the chance of at least one false positive is about 40%. **ANOVA** (analysis of variance) controls this.
Idea: compare the variation **between** group means with the variation **within** groups. If the groups differ much more than the individuals inside them, the means probably differ.
The **F-statistic** = between-group variance ÷ within-group variance. F near 1 means no evidence of a difference; large F means a small p-value.
ANOVA only tells you that *some* group differs. Use a **post-hoc** test (Tukey HSD) to find which ones.

formula.plain: How spread out the group averages are, relative to the noise inside each group.

example.title: Three call scripts
steps: Weekly sales, three agents per script: A 18, 20, 22 · B 21, 23, 25 · C 27, 29, 31
Within each group the gaps are −2, 0, +2 → SSW = 3 × 8 = 24
Tukey HSD: C beats A (p = 0.004) and B (p = 0.024); A vs B is not significant (p = 0.24)
example.result: Roll out script C. Without the post-hoc test you would not know which script to choose.

mistakes: Stopping at "significant ANOVA" without a post-hoc test.
Ignoring very unequal variances (use Welch's ANOVA).
takeaways: Post-hoc tests identify which groups differ

practice.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import f_oneway
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd
a, b, c = [18, 20, 22], [21, 23, 25], [27, 29, 31]
print(f_oneway(a, b, c))                                   # F = 15.75, p = 0.0041
print(pairwise_tukeyhsd(np.r_[a, b, c], ["A"]*3 + ["B"]*3 + ["C"]*3))
